The reel ran for nine minutes in a screening room full of men who had known him for exactly one afternoon each, and it explained nothing. The palace, the papers, the two wives, the politics, the collapse. It closed on the word he had said at the end, which nobody in the room could account for, and a title card that offered no help at all.

Nash was given the job because he was young enough not to have a stake in the answer. He drove out to a seaside nightclub and found the second wife drunk at a table at four in the afternoon, and she told him to get out of the club before he had finished his first sentence, and meant it.

So he went looking backward instead, the only direction left to him.

He read the banker Barrow's memoir in a marble library that still smelled of new paint. The old man had signed the boy over himself, once, in a mining boarding house out west, after a lodger who couldn't pay his board left behind a deed to a seam that turned out to be enormous. The mother had signed too, at the kitchen table, with the father objecting uselessly from the doorway. The boy had put a sled into Barrow's stomach hard enough to sit him down in the snow, and been taken east that same evening regardless.

On his twenty-fifth birthday the whole fortune became his, and out of all of it — mines, rail, timber — he'd asked for the one thing losing money, a newspaper called the Clarion, because he thought it might be fun. He moved a bed into the office, put a manager named Marsh on one side of him and a friend named Devlin on the other, and printed his principles on the front page over his own signature. He hired away the whole staff of the better paper across the street and threw them a party with a brass band, and danced in the middle of it himself.

He went abroad for statuary and came home engaged to the governor's niece, Adele, and the wedding was on every front page but his own. Then came the breakfasts — Nash heard about these from Marsh, who'd seen them from the doorway — a run of mornings each quieter than the last, the table lengthening until husband and wife sat at opposite ends reading rival papers, one of which he owned.

He met a shopgirl named Nora on a street corner with mud on his coat, laughing, and started calling on her rooms and telling no one. Ten days before an election Halloran, the party boss, brought Adele up those stairs and offered him a trade — withdraw, or be ruined by Monday — and was told to leave the building. He lost anyway. Devlin asked for a transfer. Adele went without either of them raising a voice.

He married Nora, and because he wanted the world to think of her as a singer, made her one, teacher and opera house and all. Devlin, brought back for the debut, got drunk instead of writing it kindly and fell asleep over half a sentence, and Emmett finished it himself, in the same cruel direction, and printed it, and fired him. Nora swallowed poison rather than go out again, and when she could speak he told her, finally, that she could stop. He shut her instead in the unfinished palace he called Silvermount, where she did jigsaw puzzles on the floor of a hall the size of a station. After a joyless picnic on a black beach and a quarrel that carried through canvas, she packed and left him.

He tore her room apart with his hands and stopped at a glass globe full of snow, said one word to no one, and carried it past a pair of facing mirrors that gave back an old man diminishing to nothing. Alone in that house he said the word again, "Bluebell," and let the globe fall. It broke on the step.

Nash sat with Marsh, with Devlin, with Nora a second time, with the old butler Colm, and put his notebook away. No single word, he decided, ever explains a life. Below him, workmen were clearing the crates from the great hall, and into the furnace, unremarked, went a small sled marked Bluebell.

He wakes with a headache and a strange flatness, and there is nobody in his head who was not there two years ago. That is not how it feels. It just feels like Tuesday.

*

She takes herself to a clinic in a shabby office building and pays to have a man taken out of her head. She signs the forms, lists the objects, says the reasons into a tape recorder in a small beige room, and does not cry until she is on the street again.

*

He gets to the platform for work and gets on the other train instead, and cannot say why. He walks out onto frozen sand and finds a woman with dyed hair already standing on it, as though the beach had been keeping her for him.

*

He goes to the bookshop to make it up with her and she looks at him the way you look at a customer. There is a young man named Peck behind the counter, and she is laughing at everything he says.

*

They drive back into the city talking too easily for strangers, and outside her building she asks him in for a drink as though it were the second time, which, for her, it isn't, and, for him, is.

*

Two friends hand him the form letter the clinic sent to everyone she knew. He takes it straight to the director's office, a man named Hallam, and asks to be given the same thing, that afternoon if possible.

*

Two years pass in small rooms and cold weather: lying on the ice of the frozen river, steam on the windows of a noodle house, the back seat at a drive-in with the sound turned down.

*

He fills two carrier bags with everything that has her in it — a hairslide, a mug, a page torn out of something — so the machine can find what the memories are pinned to.

*

The same rooms turn against them. She drinks and he counts it; he says nothing and she calls it contempt. Each of them has learned exactly which sentence does the most damage.

*

Two technicians let themselves into his flat at night. Dell puts the cap on him while he sleeps. Peck quietly slides the bagged keepsakes into his own coat, the way a magician palms a card.

*

She comes in at two in the morning having put his car into something on the way, and the row that starts over the dent finishes somewhere neither of them can come back from. She takes a bag and goes.

*

Inside his own head he stands in the worst of it — the shouting, the silences, the door — and watches each room lose its walls while he is still standing in them.

*

Rosa empties the filing cabinets on her way out of the clinic and posts every patient their own file: forms, object lists, the tape of the session where they explained what they wanted removed.

*

When the machine reaches the memories he wants to keep, he starts to run, carrying Ivy out of her own history and into places she was never in — a childhood kitchen, under a table, somewhere the map does not go.

*

Two envelopes arrive on the same morning, in the second life neither of them remembers starting twice. They sit on her stairwell and listen to their own voices tearing each other apart. She runs. She comes back up. They agree to try anyway.

*

Dell and Rosa are drinking his beer and dancing on his bed in their underwear when the map on the screen stops corresponding to anything, and neither of them notices for a long time.

*

At the end of the rail line, on a cold beach full of strangers, a man with nothing to say to anyone ends up talking to a woman with dyed hair. They break the window of a shuttered house on the shore and sleep on the boards.

*

Hallam is called out at three in the morning to put the erasure back on its rails. Rosa kisses him in the hallway. His wife, arriving behind her, tells her exactly why she has always felt that way about him, and that she has felt it before, and cannot remember why.

*

The last thing left is the shore house on the night they met. In the doorway of a room that is already going, Ivy tells him to walk out, and then to come and find her, later, at the coast.

She says it like a woman leaving a light on in a house she is about to abandon. He does not know yet that he is about to forget she ever asked.

Elias Prine sat across the desk with his hands folded, telling Martin Kray the same story twice without noticing, and Martin wrote *psychosomatic* on the form because the tests said so and the insurer wanted a reason to pay nothing. He sent the man home with an empty file and no idea what that would cost.

Martin brings Roy out to the derelict building on a pretext, walks him into the room, and puts one through his head, then photographs what's left. Satisfied.

Elias's wife moved her watch forward an hour and asked for her injection, and he gave it to her, gentle as the first time, because to him it was the first time. She asked again. He never refused her anything.

Corinne runs the plate through her friend at the registry and slides the printout across the table: Roy Mercer, in full, in ink.

Two men came through the bathroom door at night. Martin put one through the mirror and himself with him, and after that nothing new would stay where he put it.

Martin walks into a parlour with a note clenched in his fist and has the plate driven into his thigh under the five facts already carved there.

Elias's wife did not wake up the third time, and somewhere a claim that had already been denied sat in a drawer, unrelated, unread.

Martin burns the photographs of Gil, writes *he is lying to you* across Roy's picture, and copies the plate off the car outside like a man taking dictation from himself.

Martin builds a system: photographs captioned in block capitals, notes pinned to notes, facts cut into skin where they cannot be lost.

Roy sits him down and lays it out — the dealer was nobody, the revenge already taken a year gone, and the story Martin tells strangers on the telephone is not a story. It is his own house.

Roy walks him through the evidence, finds a man out past the edge of town, and stands by while Martin fires. Within minutes Martin is asking who they came to find.

Martin beats a man half his weight in a basement with water on the floor, gets a belt around his throat, and holds it.

In a rented room Martin sits with the receiver pressed to his ear, telling the Prine case to a caller who already seems to know the ending.

The dying man whispers a name that means nothing to Martin — *Elias* — and Martin takes his suit, his keys, his car, and drives away wearing another man's shape.

Out in a field Martin burns a hairbrush and a paperback, waiting to feel the end of something he cannot hold long enough to grieve.

Behind her bar Corinne watches a stranger walk in wearing clothes she recognizes, driving a car she recognizes, and she smiles and has the staff spit in his beer before it reaches him.

The voice on the phone gives him a name, a trade, an address. Martin writes it down like scripture.

She clears every pen from the house first. Then she says the things that will make him swing, waits outside for the bruises to rise, and comes back blaming a man named Vance.

Martin waits in the dark of another bathroom, takes Vance down as he comes through the door, and drives him to the edge of town at gunpoint, delivering a warning he will forget by morning.

And underneath all of it, folded into skin and photographs and burnt paper, the same unanswered thing: a claimant named Prine, a wife who tested her husband's memory until it killed her, a man who has been telling that story for a year without once hearing himself in it — until Roy says it plainly, in the last room Martin will ever let him speak in, and Martin, rather than carry the weight of being both the mourner and the man who has already mourned, burns the evidence, marks his savior as his enemy, and starts again at the beginning, certain, as always, that this time he has the right name.

THE BRIEFCASE

Marcus and Rollo drove across the city arguing about what a hamburger was called in countries where you couldn't legally smoke what you wanted. It was the kind of argument that filled the space where the job should have been. Neither of them said Tobin's name until they were standing in the corridor outside his flat, and even then they talked instead about whether a foot massage was worth being thrown off a balcony for, the gun bag hanging loose between them like something they'd forgotten to open.

They shot Tobin after Marcus said his piece from scripture, the same passage he'd say twice more before the week was out, and they took the briefcase they'd come for. A fourth man came out of the bathroom and put a full revolver's worth of rounds into the wall behind them without touching either man, and Marcus stood in the fresh pattern of holes and called it what he'd decided it was.

The briefcase went with them into the car, where Rollo's gun went off over nothing and took the head off Del in the back seat, and it went with them into Warren's garage, where a soft-spoken fixer hosed the blood out of the upholstery and put them into borrowed shorts and T-shirts, timing the whole business off a watch of his own.

It went with them into Otis's bar, delivered in those same shorts, while Otis paid an ageing boxer named Denny to go down in the fifth and told him which round to pick.

And on the way it went through a coffee shop, where two strangers had decided over eggs that nobody ever robbed a restaurant, and were up on the booth seats with a pistol out before the check came. Marcus handed over his own wallet and recited his passage a second time, explained to a frightened man with a gun what he'd decided it meant, and let the two of them walk out the door still holding nothing that mattered. He kept the briefcase in his other hand the whole time.

Denny didn't go down in the fifth. He hit the other man hard enough that the man didn't get up, and was in a taxi before the crowd worked out what it had seen. That night, in a motel on the edge of town, he asked Marielle if she'd packed his father's watch, the one a returning prisoner of war had put into his hands as a boy, the only thing his father had kept whole through years in a camp. She hadn't. It was still on the table in a flat that somebody would certainly be watching.

He went back for it anyway. He found it exactly where it had been left, and was at the counter turning it over in his hand when Rollo came out of the bathroom, and the submachine gun on the counter was nearer to Denny than Rollo's own gun was to him.

Earlier that same week Rollo had bought a bag of unusually pure heroin from a dealer named Kip and shot up before taking Otis's wife Nadia dancing at a restaurant done up like an earlier decade, where the two of them took their shoes off and won the contest. Nadia found the rest of the bag in his coat afterward, took it for something else, and had to be brought back from blue on Kip's living-room floor with a needle to the heart. She never told Otis. Rollo never got the chance to.

Driving away from his own flat with the watch back on his wrist, Denny put the car through Otis crossing at a light with a paper bag in his arms. Both wrecked; both were dragged into a pawnshop basement by men who owned the place. Denny got free, and at the door stopped, went back for a sword off the wall instead of leaving, and pulled Otis out from under a man who was raping him. Otis said they were square, so long as Denny never came back.

He collected Marielle from the motel and rode out of the city on a stolen motorcycle, the watch ticking against his wrist the whole way, carrying his father's years in the small gold weight of it.

The blood had a smell to it Danny hadn't expected—copper and salt and something sweeter underneath—and he lay on the ramp with Ash's hands on his head and thought, absurdly, of a bathroom with four dogs in it.

Pruitt had made him tell that story forty times in an empty room, a bag of drugs and four dogs and a public toilet, until the words stopped feeling like a script and started feeling like a Tuesday afternoon that had actually happened to him. "Again," Pruitt kept saying, no matter how bored Danny got, no matter how many times he protested he had it. "Tell it like you're not trying."

He'd told it to a room of professional liars in a bar and gotten the laugh in the right place, and that was the whole audition. Bram had looked at him a long moment and then nodded, and just like that Danny had a job and a name he hadn't picked.

Ren had come out of prison around the same time, years he could have shaved off by talking and hadn't, and Bram had put an envelope in his hand and a slot on the crew as if paying off a debt too old to itemize.

There had been a breakfast where eight men in black suits argued about what a pop song was really about, and whether the waitress deserved anything extra for a second pot of coffee, nobody using a real name because nobody trusted the room. Then Bram had dealt out tree names off a list in his office—Ash, Cedar, Birch, Elm—and Birch had spent a full minute complaining that his was the worst of them, as though a worse name would have saved anyone.

All of that was already behind him now, already receding into a story Danny might one day have to tell someone the way he'd told the toilet and the dogs, a memory manufactured to survive scrutiny—except this one was true, and he was bleeding out on a warehouse ramp because of it.

The job had collapsed in under a minute. Ash had put rounds through the windscreen and both side windows while the car fishtailed down the wrong street, and Danny had gone out on foot with no plan and no cover. He'd dragged a woman out of her own car and she'd had a pistol in the door pocket and used it before he got the door shut. He'd shot her. He was still shooting her, some nights, in the version of this he'd tell later, if there was a later.

Ash had gotten him here, screaming the whole way, and laid him down and sworn to him, nobody dies here today, with a conviction Danny didn't have the heart to argue with.

Birch had arrived clean and furious, insisting the police had been on the pavement before the first alarm, that someone inside had sold them, and had gone out to hide the diamonds where no one watching him could see.

Then Ren, unhurried, complaining about the noise, opening his trunk to produce a bound and terrified young officer named Doyle. Left alone with him, Ren had found an oldies station, turned it up, danced a few steps, and taken the man's ear off with a razor before dousing him in petrol, humming.

Danny had shot him from the floor with everything he had left. Then he'd told Doyle the truth—that he was police, that there were cars outside waiting for Bram—the first honest sentence he'd spoken in this building in weeks.

Cal had come back, listened, and put three rounds into Doyle to close the matter clean.

There is a version of this where the heart in Aaron's chest is only a fact he learned late, the way you learn the manufacturer of a thing you have owned for years. He is in a motel room with a man he has never met and a woman he loves and the gun is his own hand's decision, not his mind's, and afterward there is a hospital and a horn held down the whole way there.

Wes goes home to Nita and the boys' team and the certainty he used to carry like ink in his forearms, and none of it fits him the same. Lena goes home to a house with drawings still tacked to the wall, carrying something she has not decided what to call yet.

Before that, or after it, there was a pistol bought from a man in a lock-up, and a woman saying she could not breathe in the same country as somebody, saying it until it was the only furniture in the house. There was a wounding behind a motel that should have been a killing and wasn't, a hand that would not finish what it started, a man told to get up and run who instead followed the car back and stood in the doorway asking to be finished properly this time.

Somewhere in all of it a mathematician was told his heart was a number counting down, and signed a form for his wife because the freezer was all that would be left of him, and left her anyway once he was breathing again, once he had a name and a street from a man in a car park who told him this was against every rule there was and took the money regardless.

Somewhere a woman did the school run and kept the garden and had not had anything in her system for years, and a husband adored her, and two girls drew on paper that would end up taped to a kitchen wall she'd stand in front of again and again, differently, later.

Somewhere a truck came through a crossing at the wrong moment. It went on a hundred yards. It stopped, sat with the engine running, backed up a little, and then it went the rest of the way, and a man who preached to boys on Saturdays walked into a police station on his own two legs afterward, whenever afterward was, and told a sergeant what he'd done and how far he'd driven before he turned around.

A woman was taken into a side room off a corridor. First about her husband. Then, while she was still absorbing that, about both children. She started using again the way you start a job — locked bathroom doors, then the house, then the kitchen table with the drawings behind her — and it is not clear from anything you could point to whether this came before or after the meeting at the swimming pool, before or after a man followed her for a week and arranged to be in the water at her hour until it stopped looking like chance.

He told her in her own kitchen, badly, what was beating in him. She put him out that night with everything he'd brought. Four days later, or was it before the pool, or after the gun — she asked him back and he came.

He left his wife for this. Della said the true thing on his way out, that he was spending a life somebody else had paid for, and it might have been said before the pool or after the confession or in the same week he was told weeks was all he had left, the numbers laid out on a doctor's desk, the muscle finished, nothing to be done except somebody else dying at the right time.

Released early on a recommendation, a man got as far as the gate, looked at the family waiting, and kept walking, took a job cleaning rooms four hundred miles off, and none of that tells you whether it happened before the gun was bought or after, before the wounding or long after the hospital and the horn and the heart stopping on the table anyway.

What is certain: a man is dead who once was dying and then was not. A woman goes home pregnant. Another man goes home to a family he abandoned and did not abandon, in some order nobody left alive can now put back together.

Above the noise, at an open window, the old man went on talking to the younger one, patient about it, as if repeating something he had said many times before to people who never listened properly.

"Nothing survives," he said. "Not the good days, not the bad ones. Time takes them at the same rate. You understand that this isn't a complaint. It's just the arithmetic of the thing."

Below them the street was full of blue light. Two men were carried out through the crowd with their hands cuffed behind them, one shouting, one gone quiet in the particular way of a man who has stopped expecting to be listened to.

They had been arrested for what had happened in the basement a few minutes before, when Jonah had taken the fire extinguisher off the wall and gone on swinging it long after the man beneath him had stopped moving, while a few feet away, watching along with everyone else, stood the man they had actually come there for. Cort had picked the wrong face out of the dark earlier that night, seized a stranger by the arm, and had the arm turned and snapped for his trouble; the man Jonah killed was not the one whose name the two touts in the side street had sold them, pointing down towards the basement club as if it were the easiest thing in the world, once money changed hands, to say who had done it and where he drank.

They had wanted a name because of what they had walked out of the party to find — Lise on a trolley under a blanket, a face they both knew, an ambulance idling with its doors open. Before that, inside the party, Cort had been drinking past the point of being any fun, working the room, and Lise had watched him for a while without saying anything, then collected her coat and gone.

She had taken the underpass instead of crossing four lanes of headlights, and halfway along the tiled tunnel a man had a woman by the hair and was explaining something to her with his fist. The man was known, though not to Lise, as the Adder. He turned what he was doing onto her without hurrying, and when it was over he went on hitting her head against the concrete while, at the far end of the tunnel, someone looked, hesitated, and left.

Earlier, on the train down, the three of them had stood swaying together, arguing cheerfully about sex and about how much Cort had already had to drink, the kind of argument that assumes there will be a tomorrow to have it again in. That had come after an afternoon in the park, sprinklers turning over cut grass, children running through the spray, Lise lying on her side with a book she wasn't really reading and one hand resting flat on her stomach, because that morning, alone in the flat, she had sat on the edge of the bath with a stick held in both hands and let herself smile at it before telling anyone at all.

And before that there had been the bed, thin curtains, morning light, Lise telling Cort about a dream she kept having of a red tunnel she kept walking into, the two of them trading lazy insults about the man she used to live with, who was now only a friend, sitting right there, laughing along.

"You want to know what's sad," the old man said, looking down at the lights, at the men being folded into the car, "is that none of them think it's already finished. They think there's more of it coming. There's always more of it coming, until there isn't."

The younger man said nothing. Below, the doors of the car shut, and the street went on holding its light a moment longer, the way water holds a shape after the stone has already gone under.

THE DOG

I. Ruben

The house had two rooms for four adults, a baby, and a dog, and Ruben slept on the couch and watched his brother's wife move through the kitchen like something he had already decided to steal. Nestor came home from the chemist's with a scarf still smelling of smoke and knocked Alma into the counter for asking where the money had gone, and Ruben began, quietly and then not quietly, telling her she should come away with him.

The dog, Tigre, had come back off the street one night having killed something twice its size, and a neighbor told him what that was worth. Within a month it was going into the pit twice a week and coming out every time, and Ruben was hiding the winnings in the wardrobe, counting toward a version of his life that didn't include this house.

He paid two men in a bar to break his brother's ribs. Nestor worked out who'd sent them in about a day, and left with the wife, the baby, and every note Ruben had saved.

The promoter shot Tigre in the ring over a bad night's losses, and Ruben went over the rope with a knife into the man's side before he knew he was doing it, and was in the truck with Pipo and the bleeding dog before anyone moved. He ran the red light at sixty and took the side out of a small car turning across the junction.

Years later, at his brother's funeral — Nestor shot on the floor of a bank with the same scarf over his face — Ruben made the offer to Alma one last time. She looked at him the way you look at weather. No, and meant it.

II. Celine

Hector left his wife and daughters at a birthday party and moved Celine into a flat with a window facing her own billboard, so she woke up every morning across the street from her own face. She woke a second time in a hospital bed with pins holding her leg together, asking about the dog, Chispa, who was lost somewhere in the new flat's floorboards.

The lapdog's whining came up through every room until Hector tore the boards up one by one with a crowbar, and while he worked, her leg went black above him. It came off above the knee in the end. The same week, the billboard across the street was stripped bare and pasted over with someone else's face, and they sat together looking at the blank frame like a mirror with nothing in it.

She never learned who had been driving the truck.

III. Cardo

He'd been pushing a scrap cart through that same junction when the wrecks came together, and while people ran toward the wreckage he pulled the bleeding dog out of the back seat and walked away with it. He fed it by hand in a yard full of strays until it slept against him and followed him into the mornings.

A man in a good suit met him behind a church and paid him to kill his own half-brother. Cardo took the man off a pavement without trouble, then chained him to a bed frame among the empty kennels instead of finishing the job. He brought the man who'd hired him face to face with the one he'd wanted dead, set a loaded pistol on the floor exactly between them, and walked out with money from both.

He'd stood a long way back at his wife's funeral, among people who thought he'd died twenty years before, and followed his grown daughter home through three streets. He came back one day to a yard of dead strays and Tigre standing among them with its muzzle wet, put the gun to its head, and could not fire.

He got into Perla's flat while she was at work, sat on her bed an hour, and left a long confession on her machine — who he was, where he'd gone, why — and took one photograph off the shelf.

Shaved, in clothes that didn't fit him, he left the money on her table, took the dog, and walked out into the flat grey wasteland at the edge of the city, with nowhere in particular to be.

All night the helicopters went over, low and steady, spraying the fruit fly out of the fig trees and the poison down onto everybody's washing, and the whole city heard the same drone at the same hour without knowing yet what it would come to mean.

In the Hartigan house Neil changed his shirt twice while Bess worked in her studio until the last possible minute, surrounded by half-finished bodies, neither of them saying much about the guests they didn't want.

At the bakery a woman chose a cake from a book, wrote a name and an age on the card — Charlie, turning nine — and Otto promised it for Monday, please collect it promptly.

On his way to school Charlie stepped off the kerb and a waitress named Rhona, late for her shift, caught him with the wing of her car. He got up, said he was fine, refused a lift, and walked the rest of the way home insisting on it.

That night he went to sleep on the sofa and didn't wake properly. There was a room after that, a machine, and two parents taking turns in a chair. In the corridor outside it, Grant's father Duff appeared out of years of silence with a coffee he didn't drink, and because he couldn't bear the quiet, told his son about a woman from decades ago, an affair nobody in the family had ever mentioned.

Nobody came to collect the cake. Nobody paid for it either, and Otto, who was bad at being ignored, began ringing the Rill house at two in the morning just to say the boy's name into the receiver.

Across town Cheryl worked the phone from her living room, folding nappies under her chin, murmuring men through their fantasies, while her husband Stu sat three feet away going quietly incandescent. A day later he and Vern and two others walked in to the good water and found a young woman face down in the shallows. Somebody said she wasn't going anywhere and neither was the weekend, so they tied a line round her ankle and fished for two more days before telling a soul. When Vern's wife Iris heard the story told the way it got told at the pub, she stopped scrubbing her clown face off halfway through, sponge in hand, disgusted.

Vida sang every night at the club, doing the standards beautifully for people who mostly talked through them, while at home her daughter Bee practised cello into an empty house. Officer Rowe, meanwhile, needing an alibi for his time with Nan, drove the family dog to the far side of the valley and told his wife Peg it must have jumped the fence. When Nan's ex-husband Cass, a helicopter pilot, learned there was someone new in her house, he spent an afternoon sawing every chair and table and bedframe she owned into pieces.

House-sitting the Hartigan place, Ike and Dot made each other up with bruises and pale foundation and photographed themselves lying dead in the hall, laughing between shots.

At the dinner party, over the fish, Bess told Neil about the modelling session years back, and then the thing that came after it, and Neil set his glass down very carefully and made a scene in front of everyone.

Charlie's machine was switched off in the morning. That afternoon Grant and Elaine drove to the bakery to shout at Otto about his calls, and instead he sat them down, put warm bread in front of them, and the three of them grieved together over the counter.

Bee came home from rehearsal, found her mother asleep in the chair as always, walked out to the garage, pulled the door down, and started the car.

At a picnic in the hills a girl said the wrong ordinary thing, and Stu, who had been holding something since the river, picked up a rock.

Then the ground moved for eleven seconds, and by the evening bulletin all of it — the boy, the girl in the river, the girl in the hills, the wrecked furniture, the empty garage — had been folded into the same three minutes of news, as if it had all happened at once, which, by then, it nearly had.

I hadn't slept in six months when I found out that grief, someone else's grief, held on my shoulder in a folding chair, would put me under like a fist. I went four evenings a week. I was not sick. I had never been sick a day in my life, and I sat in those church halls and cried like a widower.

Then there was a stairwell, later than any of this, though I didn't know it yet — concrete steps going down into a tower's belly, and a man ahead of me with my own face turning to say something I couldn't hear, and a gun that was in his hand and then, without any distance travelled, in mine. I would get there. I didn't know I was already walking toward it.

Ada started coming to the groups and smoking through the silences, and the fraud in her showed me the fraud in me, and the sleep went. On a night flight not long after, a soap salesman named Rex Marrow talked for forty minutes about the tyranny of catalogue furniture, and I kept his card the way you keep a receipt you don't expect to need.

I needed it. My flat went up while I was away, windows on the pavement, and I called Rex from a phone box instead of calling anyone who loved me. He took me to a derelict house at the edge of the industrial district with no working plumbing and a smell like old copper.

Outside a bar he asked me to hit him as hard as I could, and we went at each other on the tarmac until we were both laughing through blood. That became Tuesdays, then a cellar, then a waiting list.

Ada overdosed and Rex brought her back to the house, and the two of them were unbearable through every floor of it while I lay downstairs rigid, though I couldn't have told you why it cost me so much to hear them.

Rex rendered stolen fat into soap on the kitchen stove and sold it back to the stores at eighty dollars a bar. He burned my hand with lye and wouldn't let me leave the minute. I used the scar as evidence and blackmailed my employer into paying me to disappear.

The cellar became Havoc — shaved heads, silence, corporate windows put in at night — and I stood in the middle of a house I had somehow built and didn't remember building.

Rex drove into oncoming traffic and let the car roll, and when I came round in the ditch he was gone, not injured, not anywhere. Then Ogden was shot outside a job with a drill still in his hand, and I started trying to shut the whole thing down.

I flew city to city closing cellars and found the same rules on the same walls everywhere, and desk clerks who looked up and called me Rex Marrow like it was the most natural thing in the world.

In a motel room, with flight records and receipts fanned over the bedspread, it went together with a horrible simplicity: one body, one account, one man, and every conversation I remembered having with him held, in fact, alone. I called Ada and asked her, badly, whose bed she'd been in. Obviously yours, she said. She asked what was wrong with me.

I found the vans under the towers, wired to the charges Havoc had been building toward all along, under the buildings that held every record of who owed what to whom. I understood, finally, what the organization had been for.

That was the stairwell. That was where I had already been going since the phone box, since the flight, since the folding chairs — down, a flight at a time, with the gun rising into my own mouth. I fired through my cheek to kill a man who had never once, technically, existed apart from me.

Ada was brought in by shaven men who apologized and left us. We held hands at the window, my face wrapped, and watched the towers go down in order, one after another, the way you'd count something off a list.

Nadir stood at the gun-shop counter with Sahar beside him, translating the forms, and the man behind the glass said something back in a voice pitched to mimic his, drawing out the vowels, and nobody in the shop laughed but nobody stopped him either. Nadir signed where he was told and did not look up.

Two men walked up the pavement outside a restaurant weeks earlier, before any of this, talking low about who was watching, then produced pistols and took a lawyer's car off him and his wife at the kerb. Paula screamed longer than was useful. Trey drove.

Later Boyle pulled over a couple for nothing at all, had them out on the hood, and put his hand where it had no business going while the husband stood three feet off and said nothing. Voss, in the passenger seat, said nothing either, that night. He said something the next morning, though — went to the commander and told him he couldn't ride with the man, and was told he could have a new car if the paperwork called it flatulence, and he signed that too.

What none of them knew yet, what hadn't happened, was a slip road on a rainy night months on, a car on its roof with the doors crumpled shut and petrol finding the exhaust, and Boyle — that same Boyle, no one else — going in through the gap on his stomach and getting the belt off Renee Hobart while she hung upside down screaming his name at him like a curse and a prayer both. He got her out before it went up. Nobody who saw it that night would have believed what his hands had done to her on the road three months before.

Mateo came to the Halstead house to change the locks after the carjacking, and Paula stood at the top of the stairs telling her husband, loud enough for the man to hear every word, that the tattooed one would have their keys copied and sold by morning. Mateo said nothing and finished the job. At Nadir's shop he fitted a new lock too, and told him the door itself was rotten at the frame, that the lock wasn't the problem. Nadir heard a man inventing extra work and told him to get out.

The insurance clerk, Delia Frank, told Boyle there was no referral for his father, not that day, not that month, and Boyle went over the desk at her with the specific violence of a man who had already lost something else that week and didn't know how to carry it. Some weeks later the shop door came off its hinges in the night exactly as the locksmith had said it would, and the insurer read the file and declined, citing the warning Nadir had ignored.

The carjacked prosecutor's car ran down a small shopkeeper named Pham on a side street; Trey and Kwame argued about it for two blocks and left him breathing outside a hospital. That same car, later, was stopped mid-theft with Clay behind the wheel of his own vehicle, four officers around him with guns drawn, until Voss walked into the middle of it and talked them down. Clay drove off anyway with Trey crouched in the seat, and three miles down the road put him out on the verge without a word.

Nadir waited outside Mateo's house that evening with the pistol in his coat, and when the door opened he raised it, and Rosie ran off the porch into her father's arms just as it went off. Nothing happened. The girl was unmarked. Sahar had bought the box that does nothing.

Voss picked up a hitchhiker in the rain, saw a hand move toward a pocket, and put two rounds into him, then burned the car with the body already in the ditch. Detective Reece was called to that ditch and stopped over the shoes. His mother, on her kitchen floor, told him she had asked him a hundred times to go and look for his brother, and he never once went.

Paula fell down her own stairs with no one home and told the housekeeper who found her that she was the only friend she had.

Trey bought a wrecked van cheap and found people in the back who had been paid for, not stock, and drove them to the docks and let them go.

The first snow came, and two cars touched at a junction, and the shouting started before anyone looked at the damage.

Solly Two Coats and his crew walked into the diamond house dressed as pilgrims, heads bowed, hands folded, and walked out with a stone the size of a bird's egg. By the time the alarm bells stopped ringing they were three streets gone.

His cousin Marv called from overseas, voice thin with wanting. Bring it straight over, he said, and Solly said he would, though he had never once done what he said he would.

In the city, Grigor the Nail had two mouths and told each a different story. To Solly he mentioned a bookmaker's shop, good odds, quiet money. To Ike and Benno, a couple of pawnbrokers with more nerve than sense, he mentioned the same shop, same hour, and let them think it was theirs alone.

Meanwhile Halloway and Digby sent their fighter Pretty Sam to buy a caravan off the travellers, a simple errand that ended with Sam flat on his back and a bare-knuckle man named Finn standing over him, knuckles split, unimpressed. With Sam useless, Halloway had no choice but to put Finn in against Coldstone's fixed bout, and swore to the gang boss that Finn would go down in the fourth.

Solly landed in the city that same week, delivered the stone to the fence Hersch for safekeeping, and carried an empty-looking case to the bookmaker's, meaning to lay a bet on the fight everyone was talking about. There Ike, Benno and a third man, Tulley, bungled their robbery entirely, tore the case and Solly's arm both away from him in the panic, and fled the shop straight into Grigor, who chased them off without knowing yet what he was chasing.

In the ring, Finn ended his man with one blow in the first round, nowhere near the fourth, and Coldstone lost a fortune he took out of Halloway's hide with his eyes alone.

Marv flew in and found no cousin, no stone, just silence, and hired a hunter called Ledge, a man who found people by finding the fools around them first.

Grigor, holding Solly and the stolen case, cut off Solly's arm to force the lock and found the case empty. He understood then that the stone had never been in it at all.

Ledge, working from the fools outward, traced the pawnbrokers, shot their car apart, and took Ike and Benno alive along with the stone they'd since recovered.

Coldstone fed what remained of Solly to his pigs and told Halloway and Digby, quite calmly, what would happen to them if the second fight went wrong.

Halloway and Digby told Finn again: fourth round. That night Coldstone's men rode out to the travellers' camp and burned Finn's mother alive in her caravan, turning a threat into a debt that could only be paid in blood.

Grigor, still hunting the stone, ambushed Ledge's car with Ike and Benno inside. In the exchange of fire Ledge died, Grigor died, and Benno died with them, the stone left rolling loose on the road.

Tulley, who had slipped away earlier with a stray dog, was the one who came back for it — and left again with the dog, which had swallowed the diamond whole sometime in the chaos, without anyone noticing.

At the rematch Finn waited, this time, until the fourth round exactly, then knocked his man cold — while the travellers moved through the crowd and cut down Coldstone's men one by one, a debt collected in full.

Halloway and Digby found Coldstone alone after the massacre and shot him where he stood. By morning the travellers and their camp had vanished as if they'd never been.

Weeks later a stray dog was handed in at a pet shop, off its food, and coughed up a stone that made the shopkeeper drop the register drawer. It was Halloway and Digby, still owed money by a dead man, who came to collect it, and left holding the diamond that had cost so many people everything.

Emlyn came to Wilder's house that same evening, still in his coat, and sat down as if he had been invited to something ordinary.

"You knew," Wilder said. "How long."

"Four years," Emlyn said. "She told me on the boat, the year you were still furnishing your little rooms. I'd had a letter delivered to the hotel desk in your hand — I know your hand better than I know my own, I've read enough of your rejections aloud to authors to recognise the loops of it. I asked her about it and she told me everything, straight through, without much drama. I said I'd always been fonder of you than of her. It seemed the truest thing to say at the time. As for your letters — I never thought much of them, if I'm honest. Too much adjective."

Wilder said nothing. He was thinking of the lunch, two years before that, when Emlyn had ordered a second bottle and spent three hours abusing the reputation of a novelist neither of them respected, needling him about the state of contemporary fiction, never once glancing toward the thing that must have sat between them like a third guest. He was thinking of dinners at that house afterward, the two of them talking cricket and racquets and school across the table while Odile passed dishes and said almost nothing, excluded from a conversation that had somehow become the real marriage in the room.

He had believed, until an hour ago, that none of that silence had contained knowledge. He had believed Odile only the night before had told her husband anything at all.

She had said as much to him herself, two years on from the rooms, in a bar with her coat still buttoned as if she meant to leave the moment she'd said it. Her marriage was over, she said, and she had spent the previous night confessing everything, at last, all of it, to Emlyn. Wilder had felt the old cowardly relief of a secret finally discharged — until she added, almost carelessly, stirring her drink, that Emlyn had for some time been publishing a writer they both quietly despised, a man whose books Wilder had the misfortune to represent. It was such an odd, unbothered thing to know that Wilder understood at once there was a whole correspondence, a whole friendship, running behind his back between the two men he had thought so separate.

That was what had made him ring Emlyn in a state, unable to keep the tremor from his own voice on the telephone, and ask him to come round.

Before any of it — before hotels and dinners and revelations — there had been an ordinary upstairs room at a party, Emlyn's own house full of noise below them, and Wilder telling Odile she was lovely while the other guests drank without them. There had been the rented rooms afterward, linen bought, plates chosen together, a small domestic republic built out of afternoons. There had been Odile's announcement that she was carrying her husband's child, and their mutual, almost bureaucratic decision that the rooms would go on precisely as before, since nothing else seemed to require changing.

And there had been, eventually, the dwindling of it — no discovery, no scene, only the crockery divided and the lease given up because upkeep of a second life had become, quietly, a chore like any other. Odile went back to the rooms once more after the confession abroad and said nothing of the trip; the afternoon passed exactly like all the others, because she had decided that some truths belonged only to the person who already possessed them.

Now, in Wilder's sitting room, the two men looked at each other across all that overlapping withholding, each having thought himself the only one managing a secret. Emlyn stood, buttoning his coat as Odile once had, unhurried.

"I don't think there's much more to say," he said. "You always did overwrite the endings."

He let himself out. Wilder sat a long while in the room where the truth had finally, uselessly, arrived, four years too late to change anything it might once have prevented.

Listen: he is unstuck in time, and so am I, telling this.

He has always known he will die by a beam weapon after speaking to a crowd, exactly as he has always known it, the way you know your own name. So when I tell you he was shot dead on a lecture platform, understand that this is not an ending, only a place the telling happens to stop.

He was small and strange as a child in a gray industrial town, the kind of boy fathers try to fix with cold water. His father threw him into the deep end of a pool once, to teach him to swim, and he sank, and at the bottom he found he did not mind staying there. He came up only because someone made him.

He does not remember which came first, the war or the marriage or the zoo. On another planet, in a transparent enclosure furnished like a nice living room, a film actress asked him what year it was on Earth, and he said he wasn't sure that question meant anything anymore. His alien captors agreed. They told him every moment that has ever existed still exists, all of it at once, a mountain range you can only see one peak of at a time from the train, and that free will was a notion peculiar to his little green planet.

He believed them enough to say so on the radio. He tried to explain the fourth dimension to a call-in audience that wanted to know about the weather. His daughter heard the broadcast and decided her father had gone senile, and began managing his checkbook and his appointments without asking him, believing this was love.

He was married once, richly, to the daughter of a man who owned an optometry school, and became a comfortable optometrist himself, and this lasted until a plane went down in the mountains. He survived the crash; his wife, driving frantically to the hospital where she thought he lay dying, was killed instead by the exhaust leaking into her own car. So the marriage ended around the same time it also, elsewhere in the great simultaneous mountain range of moments, was only beginning at an optometry school dance.

Before any of that, or after, a boy became a soldier's chaplain's assistant with no training worth mentioning, and was lost behind enemy lines with a scout who beat him whenever he asked to be left in the snow to die. They were captured. The scout's leg rotted and he died on the train east, spending his last breath naming the assistant as the reason for it. Later — or was it earlier — a fellow prisoner heard that accusation and promised, quite calmly, that the debt would be collected one day, no hurry, he had all the time in the world to arrange it.

In a camp full of enemy officers fat on rations some clerk had never corrected, he waited. Then he was moved to a great city and put with other prisoners underground in a disused meat locker that still smelled of the animals it once held. That night the city burned to nothing above their heads. They came up into ash and found streets that used to be there weren't. They spent days digging bodies from cellars until one of the diggers died simply from the dry heaving of it, his body refusing the job his hands kept doing.

He came home and collapsed and was hospitalized, and a fellow patient there gave him lurid paperbacks by a hack writer of other worlds, which he read without much interest, not yet knowing how useful that furniture of thought would later prove.

None of this arranges itself. He told it to me out of order because it came to him out of order, a man already shot standing at a lectern describing his own assassination to a crowd as a fact of the fourth dimension, calm, unsurprised, already elsewhere, already everywhere the story had ever put him.

Listen: he is unstuck in time, and so am I, telling this.

He has always known he will die by a beam weapon after speaking to a crowd, exactly as he has always known it, the way you know your own name. So when I tell you he was shot dead on a lecture platform, understand that this is not an ending, only a place the telling happens to stop.

He was small and strange as a child in a gray industrial town, the kind of boy fathers try to fix with cold water. His father threw him into the deep end of a pool once, to teach him to swim, and he sank, and at the bottom he found he did not mind staying there. He came up only because someone made him.

He does not remember which came first, the war or the marriage or the zoo. On another planet, in a transparent enclosure furnished like a nice living room, a film actress asked him what year it was on Earth, and he said he wasn't sure that question meant anything anymore. His alien captors agreed. They told him every moment that has ever existed still exists, all of it at once, a mountain range you can only see one peak of at a time from the train, and that free will was a notion peculiar to his little green planet.

He believed them enough to say so on the radio. He tried to explain the fourth dimension to a call-in audience that wanted to know about the weather. His daughter heard the broadcast and decided her father had gone senile, and began managing his checkbook and his appointments without asking him, believing this was love.

He was married once, richly, to the daughter of a man who owned an optometry school, and became a comfortable optometrist himself, and this lasted until a plane went down in the mountains. He survived the crash; his wife, driving frantically to the hospital where she thought he lay dying, was killed instead by the exhaust leaking into her own car. So the marriage ended around the same time it also, elsewhere in the great simultaneous mountain range of moments, was only beginning at an optometry school dance.

Before any of that, or after, a boy became a soldier's chaplain's assistant with no training worth mentioning, and was lost behind enemy lines with a scout who beat him whenever he asked to be left in the snow to die. They were captured. The scout's leg rotted and he died on the train east, spending his last breath naming the assistant as the reason for it. Later — or was it earlier — a fellow prisoner heard that accusation and promised, quite calmly, that the debt would be collected one day, no hurry, he had all the time in the world to arrange it.

In a camp full of enemy officers fat on rations some clerk had never corrected, he waited. Then he was moved to a great city and put with other prisoners underground in a disused meat locker that still smelled of the animals it once held. That night the city burned to nothing above their heads. They came up into ash and found streets that used to be there weren't. They spent days digging bodies from cellars until one of the diggers died simply from the dry heaving of it, his body refusing the job his hands kept doing.

He came home and collapsed and was hospitalized, and a fellow patient there gave him lurid paperbacks by a hack writer of other worlds, which he read without much interest, not yet knowing how useful that furniture of thought would later prove.

None of this arranges itself. He told it to me out of order because it came to him out of order, a man already shot standing at a lectern describing his own assassination to a crowd as a fact of the fourth dimension, calm, unsurprised, already elsewhere, already everywhere the story had ever put him.
